title: Lodging house rules approved, short-term rental bylaw deferred
subtitle: Heritage designation of 91 Madison Avenue South, rental replacement by-law, Bramm Yards, and arts funding advocacy.
overview: Council approved the planning changes that allow lodging houses city-wide wherever residential uses are permitted {{vote:m21}}. It held back the licensing by-law that covered both lodging houses and Airbnb-style short-term rentals. Staff will return in August with a revised lodging house by-law and its staffing needs, and the short-term rental rules will be reviewed with hosts, tenants and insurers and reported on before the end of 2024 {{vote:m4}}.

Council also confirmed its intention to designate 91 Madison Avenue South under the Ontario Heritage Act, over an objection from the property's owner {{vote:m5}}. It approved a Rental Replacement By-law to help protect tenants when rental buildings are redeveloped {{vote:m26}}, and approved a plan for the Bramm Yards site, including a market assessment before the land is offered for sale {{vote:m16}}.

Council sent a letter asking the federal government to raise arts funding {{vote:m28}}. It put off a motion urging the province to act on renovictions until the August 12 special meeting {{vote:m29}}. It also approved a settlement authorization on an Ontario Land Tribunal appeal after a closed session {{vote:m36}}.

decisions.detail: Council adopted the Official Plan amendments and approved the zoning changes to permit lodging houses city-wide wherever residential uses are permitted {{vote:m21}}.

Staff must return in August with a revised lodging house by-law and staffing needs, while short-term rental provisions are deferred for further review of insurance, room limits, fees, the 90-day limit and tenant codes, with a report before the end of 2024 {{vote:m4}}.
Council affirmed its intention to designate the property under Part IV of the Ontario Heritage Act, declined to withdraw the notice, and approved the designation by-law {{vote:m5}}.
Council approved the by-law with related Official Plan and demolition control amendments, and asked staff to continue work on a tenant assistance policy and report back in June 2025 {{vote:m26}}.

Council approved the revised vision, allocated up to $400,000 from the Environmental Remediation Reserve for pre-design reports, and directed a market assessment, with scoring and evaluation details to come back to Council before a public request for proposals is issued {{vote:m16}}.
Council asked the Department of Canadian Heritage to increase Canada Council for the Arts funding and move to a regional funding model, with support letters to the Minister and area MPs {{vote:m28}}.
Council deferred the motion urging the province to strengthen tenant protections against renovictions to the August 12, 2024 Special Council meeting {{vote:m29}}.
Council deferred the 2024 pilot allowing alcohol in select parks and directed staff to keep working with police and monitor provincial changes.

debate: Short-term rental hosts said the proposed rules would push them out. Their concerns were the $2M insurance with the City named as insured, which they said means costly commercial coverage, and the licence fee, the 90-day limit, a four-bedroom cap, and a public registry of addresses.

Staff said inspections would be pre-arranged or invited by a tenant, and that the public registry would list only the address, licence status and last inspection date, not owner details. They said the proposed by-law was the least restrictive among comparable Ontario municipalities and that the insurance terms came from the City's insurance pool.

Some councillors favoured deferral to allow more engagement and to clarify insurance costs. One councillor said costs could be passed on to renters and reduce supply when vacancy is low, and that the timing was wrong. Others wanted lodging house licensing to move ahead quickly.

On 91 Madison Avenue South, a church representative said designation would bring heavy costs for doors and windows. Staff said exact replacement is not required, interiors are excluded, heritage permits carry no fee, and grants are available.

On the renoviction motion, one councillor said it was a long advocacy motion that staff had not fully reviewed and the full effect on landlords was unclear. Supporters said it built on Council's earlier lobbying and the new rental replacement by-law, and the deferral allowed staff review.
